levels.title: Level 1: Runtime Polymorphism — Replace Conditionals
levels.description: Polymorphism at runtime means the correct behavior is chosen through a shared contract (interface or abstract class), not through if/else or switch on type strings. Refactor tight coupling into plug-in strategies.

questions.text: PaymentProcessor uses switch(type) to call chargeCard() or transferFunds(). Which refactor lets you add new payment types without editing PaymentProcessor?
choices: Introduce a PaymentStrategy interface with a unified execute(double amount) method that all payment classes implement
Rename both payment classes to PaymentUtil and merge their methods into one class
Add more branches to the switch statement and document each type in a wiki
questions.correct_answer: Introduce a PaymentStrategy interface with a unified execute(double amount) method that all payment classes implement
questions.explanation: Runtime polymorphism through an interface lets the processor depend on behavior, not concrete types. New payment classes implement the same contract and plug in without touching orchestration code.

questions.text: Concrete classes now implement PaymentStrategy.execute(). Which TWO practices prevent silent override bugs at compile time?
choices: Mark implementing methods with @Override (or the language equivalent) so the compiler verifies the signature
Keep subclass method visibility at least as accessible as the interface method (public stays public)
Rename execute() to executePayment() in one subclass only to clarify intent
Declare interface methods private so each subclass can define its own visibility
correct_answer: Mark implementing methods with @Override (or the language equivalent) so the compiler verifies the signature
Keep subclass method visibility at least as accessible as the interface method (public stays public)
questions.explanation: @Override catches typos and signature drift early. Narrowing visibility breaks substitutability — code expecting PaymentStrategy would fail when given a subclass that hides the method.

questions.text: Product requests CryptoPayment support. With polymorphism in place, what is the correct change?
choices: Add CryptoPayment as a new class implementing PaymentStrategy; PaymentProcessor stays unchanged
Open PaymentProcessor and add another switch branch for crypto
Delete PaymentStrategy and copy-paste execute() logic into PaymentProcessor
questions.correct_answer: Add CryptoPayment as a new class implementing PaymentStrategy; PaymentProcessor stays unchanged
questions.explanation: OCP in action: extend by adding a new implementation class. The client (PaymentProcessor) continues to call execute() on the interface — zero modification risk to production orchestration.

levels.title: Level 2: Compile-Time Polymorphism — Method Overloading
levels.description: Compile-time polymorphism (method overloading) resolves the correct method at compile time based on parameter types and arity — within a single class. It is not substitutable runtime polymorphism; know when each applies.

questions.text: A teammate suggests using method overloading in ReportExporter: export(Report), export(Report, PDFOptions), export(Report, CSVOptions). What kind of polymorphism is this?
choices: Compile-time polymorphism (static overloading) — the compiler picks the method by signature at build time
Runtime polymorphism (dynamic overriding) — the JVM picks the method while the program is running based on object type
Neither — overloading is just syntactic sugar with no design meaning
questions.correct_answer: Compile-time polymorphism (static overloading) — the compiler picks the method by signature at build time
questions.explanation: Overloading binds at compile time within one class. Overriding binds at runtime when a subclass replaces a parent or interface method. Confusing the two leads to fragile designs.

questions.text: Which TWO situations are appropriate uses of method overloading rather than an interface hierarchy?
choices: Convenience defaults: export(report) delegates to export(report, defaultOptions)
Same operation, different parameter shapes in one cohesive class (e.g., format-specific option types)
Adding a completely new payment provider that must plug in without recompiling the processor
Replacing a switch on class type inside a loop over unrelated subclasses
correct_answer: Convenience defaults: export(report) delegates to export(report, defaultOptions)
Same operation, different parameter shapes in one cohesive class (e.g., format-specific option types)
questions.explanation: Overloading suits variations of one responsibility in a single class. Plug-in behavior across types that evolve independently belongs to runtime polymorphism via interfaces.

questions.text: The team adds export(Report, String format) alongside export(Report, PDFOptions). Call sites become ambiguous and bugs slip in. What is the clean-code fix?
choices: Remove the String overload; use typed option objects or an enum Format so the compiler can distinguish signatures safely
Add more String overloads for every format until developers memorize the order
Convert ReportExporter into an abstract class with one abstract export method per format
questions.correct_answer: Remove the String overload; use typed option objects or an enum Format so the compiler can distinguish signatures safely
questions.explanation: Overloading fails when parameters are too similar (String vs String). Prefer strong types or enums. If formats behave differently at runtime with plug-in extensibility, switch to a Strategy interface instead.

levels.title: Level 3: Inheritance Polymorphism & Liskov Substitution
levels.description: Subtype polymorphism through inheritance lets clients treat subclasses as their parent type. Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) requires subclasses to honor the parent's contract without surprising behavior.

questions.text: BillingService currently depends on three concrete employee classes. What refactor lets charge() work for any employee type present or future?
choices: Make BillingService depend on Employee (abstract base or interface) and call calculatePay() polymorphically
Add a fourth copy of charge() logic for each new employee type inside BillingService
Store employees as JSON strings and parse type at runtime inside charge()
questions.correct_answer: Make BillingService depend on Employee (abstract base or interface) and call calculatePay() polymorphically
questions.explanation: The client should depend on the shared Employee abstraction. Each subtype overrides calculatePay() with its own rules while BillingService stays a single loop.

questions.text: A subclass Intern.calculatePay() throws an exception when hours > 8, while Employee's contract implies pay is always computable. Which TWO statements describe the LSP violation and fix?
choices: Subclasses must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions in ways that break callers expecting Employee behavior
Replace the throws with valid pay logic for overtime rules, or model Intern outside the Employee hierarchy if rules differ fundamentally
LSP only applies to interfaces, not abstract classes, so Intern may behave however it wants
Fix LSP by making calculatePay() return null instead of throwing
correct_answer: Subclasses must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions in ways that break callers expecting Employee behavior
Replace the throws with valid pay logic for overtime rules, or model Intern outside the Employee hierarchy if rules differ fundamentally
questions.explanation: LSP means any Employee reference must work wherever Employee is expected. Surprise exceptions or stricter rules break BillingService. Either honor the contract or use composition/separate types.

questions.text: Employee needs a shared validateTimesheet() implementation reused by all subtypes, plus a subtype-specific calculatePay(). Which abstraction fits best?
choices: Abstract class Employee with concrete validateTimesheet() and abstract calculatePay()
Interface Employee with default validateTimesheet() only — no fields allowed anywhere
Final class Employee with public static calculatePayFor(type, hours) switch method
questions.correct_answer: Abstract class Employee with concrete validateTimesheet() and abstract calculatePay()
questions.explanation: Abstract classes share code and state across a true IS-A hierarchy. Interfaces excel at pure behavior contracts. Mixed shared logic plus overriding favors an abstract base; pure plug-in behavior favors interfaces.

levels.title: Level 4: Composing Polymorphism — Strategy, Factory & Injection
levels.description: Production systems compose polymorphism: a factory or registry selects the concrete strategy at runtime, and dependency injection supplies it to the client. The client never instantiates concrete types.

questions.text: CheckoutController uses new CreditCardPayment() inside checkout(). How should PaymentStrategy be supplied so the controller stays testable and decoupled?
choices: Inject PaymentStrategy through the constructor or setter; CheckoutController only calls strategy.execute()
Use a static singleton PaymentStrategy.getInstance() accessed from every method
Import concrete classes directly and pick one with Math.random() at runtime
questions.correct_answer: Inject PaymentStrategy through the constructor or setter; CheckoutController only calls strategy.execute()
questions.explanation: Injection inverts the dependency: the orchestrator receives an abstraction. Tests can inject mocks; production wiring chooses the real strategy elsewhere.

questions.text: Users pick a payment method at checkout time. Which TWO patterns correctly select the concrete PaymentStrategy without polluting CheckoutController?
choices: PaymentStrategyFactory.create(PaymentMethod method) returns the matching implementation
A registry Map keyed by PaymentMethod enum that maps to strategy instances
CheckoutController switch(method) { case CARD: return new CreditCardPayment() }
Global static variable set to whichever payment class loaded last
correct_answer: A registry Map keyed by PaymentMethod enum that maps to strategy instances
questions.explanation: Object creation for polymorphic families belongs in a factory or registry — one place to extend when CryptoPayment arrives. Controllers orchestrate; they should not construct concrete strategies.

questions.text: CryptoPayment launches tomorrow. CheckoutController and PaymentStrategyFactory already exist. What is the minimal, OCP-compliant change?
choices: Implement CryptoPayment, register it in the factory/registry, add CRYPTO to PaymentMethod — CheckoutController unchanged
Rewrite CheckoutController.checkout() to handle blockchain receipts inline
Remove PaymentStrategy and inline all payment logic back into the controller for clarity
questions.correct_answer: Implement CryptoPayment, register it in the factory/registry, add CRYPTO to PaymentMethod — CheckoutController unchanged
questions.explanation: Composed polymorphism pays off here: new behavior is a new class plus wiring in the factory. The controller, tests, and API surface stay stable — the hallmark of mature runtime polymorphism.
